clinicalPearls: Caused by Cryptococcus, a genus of yeast-like fungi; WHO declared C. neoformans a critical priority pathogen in 2022 (p.1703).
C. neoformans and C. gattii are now regarded as species complexes; for clinical purposes both cause indistinguishable disease termed cryptococcosis (p.1703-1704).
High-risk hosts for C. neoformans: hematologic malignancy, solid-organ transplant, advanced liver disease, diabetes, glucocorticoid therapy, and advanced HIV with CD4+ counts <200/uL (p.1704).
C. gattii disease is NOT generally associated with specific immune deficits and often occurs in immunocompetent individuals; associated with autoantibodies to GM-CSF (p.1704).
Disease usually presents as pulmonary disease and/or chronic meningoencephalitis, but cryptococcosis can affect any tissue or organ (p.1704-1705).

Cryptococcal meningitis differs from bacterial meningitis: many patients present with symptoms of several weeks' duration and classic meningismus may be absent; indolent cases can present as subacute dementia or depression (p.1705).
In AIDS patients, cryptococcal meningitis is the initial AIDS-defining illness in ~2% and generally occurs with CD4+ counts <100/uL; about one-third also have pulmonary disease (p.1606).

Diagnosis requires demonstration of cryptococcal cells or antigen in normally sterile tissue; India ink of CSF shows encapsulated yeast and CRAg (serum/CSF) is both sensitive and specific with rapid point-of-care lateral flow assays (p.1705).
Increased intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis is managed by repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures and shunt placement; mannitol and acetazolamide are NOT effective (p.1706).
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) can occur after starting ART in HIV; recommended to start ART 4-6 weeks after initiating antifungal therapy (p.1706).
Serum CRAg screening is recommended for asymptomatic people with HIV and CD4+ counts <100-200/uL to identify those at high risk of cryptococcal disease (p.1705-1706).
harrison.pathophysiology: Cryptococcal infection is almost always acquired by inhalation of aerosolized particles (small desiccated yeast cells or basidiospores); occasionally by direct skin inoculation. C. neoformans is found in soils contaminated with avian (pigeon) excreta, whereas C. gattii inhabits arboreal species such as eucalyptus and is not found in bird feces. Infection is acquired in childhood and is common, but disease is rare in the absence of impaired immunity, indicating that intact pulmonary defenses effectively contain the fungus. Some infections lead to latency with viable organisms harbored in granulomas. Extrapulmonary dissemination to the CNS may occur via direct fungal migration across endothelium and via macrophage 'Trojan horse' carriage. Virulence factors include the antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule, melanin production, and enzymes (phospholipase, urease). Copious release of capsular polysaccharide into tissues interferes with local immune responses, and infection may elicit little or no inflammatory response; capsular polysaccharide is the antigen measured diagnostically (p.1704).
additionalDifferentials: Subacute dementia or depression (indolent CNS cryptococcosis mimic)
Pulmonary malignancy or other causes of lung nodules/masses (pulmonary cryptococcosis found incidentally on chest radiograph)
infectionMimics: Molluscum contagiosum (cutaneous cryptococcosis in highly immunosuppressed patients resembles its lesions)
Other disseminated/endemic fungal infections (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis)
additionalInvestigations: CSF examination: opening pressure, protein, glucose, cell count, Gram stain, cultures
India ink stain of CSF for encapsulated yeast
Cryptococcal antigen (CRAg) assay in CSF and blood; point-of-care lateral flow assay
Fungal cultures of CSF and blood (blood cultures often positive)
Serum CRAg screening in HIV with low CD4+ counts
PCR (confirm positive or negative results with independent methods such as CRAg and culture)
Chest imaging for pulmonary disease (nodules, infiltrates, masses)
Biopsy for CNS cryptococcoma or to distinguish inadequately treated infection from immune reconstitution syndrome
redFlags: Raised intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis requiring serial therapeutic lumbar puncture drainage (and possible shunt placement)
Sudden catastrophic vision loss from meningeal cryptococcosis
Cranial nerve paresis, vision and hearing loss
Altered mental status, headache, and blurred vision as clues to elevated ICP
Refractory cryptococcosis despite antifungal therapy (prompt susceptibility testing)
harrison.prognosis: Even with antifungal therapy, cryptococcosis carries high morbidity and mortality. The most important prognostic factors are the extent and duration of the underlying immunologic deficit. Disease is often curable in those with no apparent immune dysfunction, but in irreversible immunosuppression the goal is remission maintained by lifelong suppressive therapy. Before ART, median survival for AIDS patients with cryptococcosis was <1 year. Cryptococcosis with underlying neoplastic disease has a particularly poor prognosis. Poor prognostic markers for CNS disease: positive India ink on initial CSF exam (heavy fungal burden), high CSF pressure, low CSF glucose, low CSF pleocytosis (<2/uL), recovery of yeast from extraneural sites, absence of antibody to capsular polysaccharide, CSF or serum cryptococcal antigen level >=1:32, and concomitant glucocorticoid therapy or hematologic malignancy. Relapse is common even with relatively intact immunity (p.1706).
pitfalls: India ink and Gram stain may be falsely negative with low fungal burden or misread as positive by inexperienced operators (p.1705).
CRAg is often negative in pulmonary cryptococcosis, so it is less useful for diagnosing pulmonary disease and of only limited use in monitoring response to therapy (p.1705).
Cryptococcal cells with negative cultures on CSF staining and persistently elevated CSF/blood cryptococcal antigen long after culture clearance do NOT indicate treatment failure (p.1705).
Categorizing cryptococcosis as 'extrapulmonary without CNS involvement' should be made only after CSF evaluation reveals no evidence of cryptococcal infection (p.1705).

Prophylactic dexamethasone in HIV-associated cryptococcosis is NOT recommended (associated with reduced fungal clearance and increased mortality); glucocorticoids are not helpful for raised ICP unless from a mass lesion with edema (p.1706).
Echinocandins are NOT effective against Cryptococcus species (p.1706).
IRIS can be difficult to distinguish from relapsing/refractory infection (p.1706).
harrison.severityClassification: Nonsevere disease limited to the lungs or other non-CNS sites is distinguished from severe disease or CNS involvement; severe/CNS cryptococcosis is treated with induction, consolidation, and maintenance phases (p.1705).
management: Treat meningoencephalitis and severe disease with induction antifungal therapy combining liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine
Follow induction with consolidation and prolonged maintenance therapy using the azole fluconazole
Control raised intracranial pressure in meningitis with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures and cerebrospinal fluid diversion where needed

Address the underlying immune deficit by starting or optimising antiretroviral therapy in HIV, timed to reduce immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, and by reducing immunosuppression where feasible
Screen for cryptococcal antigenaemia in advanced HIV and give pre-emptive fluconazole to those who are antigen-positive without meningitis
Monitor response with follow-up cerebrospinal fluid cultures and repeat pressure measurement
Coordinate care with infectious diseases specialists and, for large lesions or hydrocephalus, neurosurgery
